title: Christmas: the Word again (John 1:14)
hookLine: at Christmas, churches read John's prologue: the Word became flesh
tomorrow: Year two close: the book in your hands

cards: Two Christmas readings, and they could hardly be more different. One is from Luke: shepherds, a manger, angels over the fields at night. The other is from John, and it has no manger at all.
No shepherds, no star, no inn. It starts before time: in the beginning was the Word.

In many churches, Luke's story is read at night, and John's opening on Christmas morning, or as the last reading at a candlelit service of lessons and carols. Today, the one verse in John that makes it a Christmas text.

teach.h: IN THE BEGINNING WAS THE WORD.
teach.b: John's Gospel opens the way Genesis does.

teach.h: SARX: THE PLAIN WORD FOR FLESH.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." The Word, in Greek the logos: speech, reason, the meaning behind everything.
Then: "And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not."

And the verse the passage leans toward, verse fourteen: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth."
You met this verse in the autumn, through its tent: dwelt, in Greek, is pitched his tent. At Christmas, churches lean on the other word. Flesh.
In Greek, sarx, the plain word for the stuff of bodies. John could have said the Word appeared, or visited. He says it became flesh.
Not an idea, not a voice from the sky.

teach.h: A BABY WHO HAS TO BE FED.
teach.b: At Christmas that flesh is a baby: someone who has to be fed, changed, carried and kept warm. Christians say the Word that was there in the beginning started out that small.
Churches keep the day a little differently. Many celebrate on December twenty-fifth; many Orthodox churches that follow the older Julian calendar celebrate on what is now January seventh.

Catholic, Anglican and many Protestant churches read this prologue on Christmas Day. In the Orthodox liturgy for the Nativity, the Gospel is Matthew's story of the Magi, and John's prologue is read at Easter.
Luke tells you where he was born. John tells you who was born.

how: In Catholic, Anglican and many Protestant churches, John 1:1–14 is read on Christmas Day and often as the last lesson at services of lessons and carols; Orthodox churches read Matthew's account of the Magi at the Nativity and John's prologue at Easter.

games.q: you're John, writing the story of Jesus. the other Gospels tell of his birth and family. where do you begin?
o: with a list of his ancestors.
games.why: "In the beginning was the Word." John starts before creation, echoing Genesis, and only then: the Word was made flesh.

practice: If you can, turn the lights down, light one lamp or candle safely, and read John 1:1–14 slowly, looking at the flame for a breath when you reach the light shining in the darkness.

When you reach the Word made flesh, think of one ordinary body you love, a hand, a face, a child asleep; Christians say God came that close. If you pray, read verse fourteen once more, slowly, as your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Christmas. The feast of the birth of Jesus, when John's Gospel says the Word was made flesh and pitched his tent among us.
